title: Switching away from Google Maps : Here Maps, Bing Maps, OpenStreetMap...
description: I'm still looking for alternatives to popular Google services, just to see if it would be feasible to not have all my data in one provider's hand. In this one, I'm going to take a look at map services.  Google Maps Google maps is widely known. It's probably the richest map data-wise, with the added benefit of street view, a well-stocked satellite view, data from points of interest and businesses, and a good interface. We're going to take a look at other services, with the requirements that they use something other than Google maps for data. I'm not expecting a Street view replacement in any of these alternatives.  Open Street Maps OSM is like the wikipedia of maps, with anyone being able to contribute to it, trace roads, buildings, and add points of interests, and more. OSM is accessible from their website, www.openstreetmap.org, and has the basics, such as directions, and search. It lacks a satellite view, street view, and doesn't have any informations about businesses. It also doesn't have the most elegant tile set there is.  MapQuest uses the OSM database to build their maps. It's been around for a while, but it seems more focused on the US market.  Qwant Maps use OSM as well, but it's still an alpha-level product. It doesn't have a mobile application, and doesn't have directions yet. It does look nice, and has basic informations when clicking on any POI, with favorites support.  On smartphones, the choice is a bit more varied, and that's what matters. OSMAnd seems to be the best choice out there on Android, with downloadable maps for offline access, and a ton of different options including which points of interest you want to display, the look of the map, a dark theme, a car GPS mode, and many more.  It's also interesting to note that there is a project called Open Street Cam which aims to provide an alternative to Street View.  Here Maps Here Maps was formerly a Nokia product. They provide a web interface, as well as a mobile app, called Here We Go. The web interface is pretty slow to load tiles, and returned a very limited set of Point of interests, in my tests. It does have a few informations on each of them, though, so that's a plus.  It has directions, which are actually pretty well done, letting you choose between car, bike, on foot, as well as ride sharing or even a taxi. It also has a satellite view, and can even show some public transportation information. Here maps also have access to traffic information in certain cities.  The mobile app is alright, it is pretty clear right at startup about what kind of data it collects, and has most of what you'd expect, including directions, favorites, and traffic data. It also can change the view mode from normal to satellite, and even download offline maps, if you're preparing a trip abroad and want to make sure you'll get a functioning GPS service.  Here maps is a good proposition that could definitely replace Google Maps in my admitedly simple uses.  Bing Maps Bing Maps is Microsoft's map service. It's a smaller proposition, including only a web interface and no mobile application. Bing maps has points of interest with a lot of data supplied by TripAdvisor, and local data providers, such as Pages Jaunes in France. It has pretty complete directions, including the ability to avoid highways or ferries, and it has traffic data to help you navigate or use it as a GPS while driving.    Bing Maps also supports a satellite view, and what they call "streetside", which is a street view equivalent. It seems to work in major cities, for example, in France, Paris had a pretty good coverage, but this feature is not available as widely as Google's.  Bing Maps doesn't seem to have a mobile application though, which is a shame, since it's where most people will use it anyway.  All in all, Bing maps is probably the best proposition on the web, outside of Google Maps, but without a mobile application to use, I just could not see myself switching to it.  Other alternatives The first is Wikimapia, a collaborative effort to give free maps to anyone who might need them. It's distributed under the open source Creative Communs BY-SA license.   Yandex Maps is also a good proposition, but if you're trying to escape the internet giants, the Russian Google might not be the best choice.  Duck Duck Go uses Apple Maps, which looks good, but they don't provide a separate map service.  All in all, while Here Maps and Bing Maps are pretty good, I still feel they lack the polish and overall nice finish of Google Maps. Their tilesets look a bit dated and bland, and even though data-wise, they don't seem to lag behind Gmaps too much, presentation matters, and the user experience is not as polished. They both are perfectly usable though.  Qwant Maps might one day have a user experience closer to the one Google delivers, but as of now, it's just not ready. For now, I'll replace Google Maps with Here Maps, but I'm not 100% satisfied.   Follow me on Twitter : http://twitter.com/thelinuxEXP

asr.full_text: Hey guys, this is Nick and welcome to my Linux experiment. I'm still looking for alternatives to popular Google services, just to see if it would be feasible to not have all of my data in one provider's hands. In this one, I'm gonna take a look at map services. Google Maps Well, Google Maps is widely known. It's probably the richest map data wise, with the added benefits of Street View, a well-stocked satellite view, data from points of interest and businesses, and a good legible interface. It also comes with a mobile application, which is the primary way to interact with maps. We're going to take a look at other services, with the requirements that they use something other than Google Maps for data, that they are available as a mobile app or at least a mobile website, and I'm not expecting a Street View replacement in any of these alternatives since the cost is prohibitive. OpenStreetMaps. OSM is like the Wikipedia of maps, with anyone being able to contribute to it, trace roads, buildings and app points of interests and more. It has a vibrant community and serves as the base for a lot of mapping services and applications. OSM is accessible from their website openStreetMap.org and has the basics such as directions and search. It lacks a satellite view, streetview and doesn't have any information about businesses, which is uses besides simple routing. It also doesn't have the most elegant tile-set there is. The colors are muted, it lacks legibility and is generally not very appealing. Fortunately, since OSM is open-source, a few providers have built their own tile-sets and features off of it. You most notably can use GNOME Maps or Marble to access it from the desktop app on Linux. So what map provider use OpenStreetMaps? Well, we get MapQuest, which uses the OpenStreetMap database to build their maps. It's been around for a while, but it seems more focused on the US market, and doesn't return any useful data for France, for example. Quantmaps uses OSM as well, and it's still an alpha-level product. It doesn't have a mobile application product, doesn't have an app and not yet got directions. It does look nice, and has basic information when clicking on any path with favourite support but is just too limited. This might, at some point, be a very valid alternative, but for now, it just lacks too many features. As of now there doesn't seem to be a full-on web implementation of OpenStreetMaps with Points of Interests, Directions, and Satellite View. OpenStreetMap is mostly used by service providers to sell this kind of package for integration in other services, but they don't seem to provide a free online mapping service. On smartphones, the choice is a bit more varied, and that's what matters, because this is where you're going to be using these maps most of the time. OSM ONT seems to be the best choice out there on Android with downloadable maps for offline access, and a ton of different options, including which point of interest you wanna display, the look of the map, a dark theme, a car GPS mode, and many more… It's also interesting to note that there is a project called OpenStreetCam, which aims to provide an alternative to Streetview, but its interface is a bit cumbersome and, since it's sourced by users, it's not as complete and well detailed. Still it's a great project that should definitely be integrated directly into the OSM interface to give it more visibility. HairMaps HairMaps was formerly a Nokia product and is now operated by a consortium of auto manufacturers they provide a web interface as well as a mobile app called here we go the web interface is pretty slow to load tiles and return a very limited set of point of interests in my tests it does have a few informations on each of them though so there's a plus. It has directions, which are actually pretty well done, letting you choose between car, bike, on foot, as well as ride-sharing or even a taxi. It also has a satellite view and can even show some public transportation information, such as the path they will take. In my hometown, Brest, I could see the itinerary their streetcars take, but not the bus lines. And in Paris they have all metro lines for example. Heron Maps also have access to traffic information in certain cities but it does not have a Street View implementation. The mobile application called here we go is alright, it is pretty clear right at start up about what kind of data it collects and it has most of what you'd expect, including directions, favorites and traffic data. It also can change the view mode from Normal to Satellite and even download off-line maps if you're preparing a trip abroad and want to make sure you'll get a functioning GPS service. Here Maps doesn't look very good in my opinion, but it gets the job done. In general it's not a bad service, but the slow loading of tiles and the inertia while dragging the map was a bit annoying. HairMaps is a good proposition that could definitely replace Google Maps in my admittedly simple uses. Bing Maps Bing Maps is Microsoft's Map service. It is a smaller proposition, including only a web interface and no mobile application. Bing Maps has points of interest with a lot of data supplied by Tripadvisor, and local data providers such as Pagone in France. It has pretty complete directions, including the ability to avoid highways or ferries and it has traffic data to help you navigate or use it as a GPS while driving Bing maps supports satellite view, and what they call Streetsight which is a Street View equivalent It seems to work in major cities, for example in France, Paris has a good coverage. But this feature isn't as widely available as Google's Bing Maps doesn't seem to have a mobile application though, which is a shame. Since it's one where most people will use it anyway More aggravating? There is no mobile version of Bing Maps at all, not even a mobile website or at least I couldn't find it. This is a big oversight that makes the service instantly less accessible and useful. All in all, Bing maps is probably the best proposition on the web outside of Google Maps but without a mobile application to use I just could not see myself switching to it. Other alternatives. Apart from these big ones, there are a few other alternatives that deserve a mention. The first is Wikimapia, a collaborative effort to give free maps to anyone who might need them. It's distributed under the open-source Creative Commons BYSA license. While its interface is not up to par and the data volume seems pretty low where I live it's definitely something to keep an eye on. Yandex maps is also a good proposition but if you're trying to escape the internet giants the Russian Google might not be the best choice for you. DuckduckGo uses apple maps which looks good, but they don't provide a separate map service. It's just used to illustrate and locate their search results. You can't actually use the map as you would google maps. You are limited to browsing it, switching the view but it doesn't have any directions or point of interest details. All in all, while hero maps and big maps are pretty good I still feel they like the polish and overall nice finish of Google Maps. Their tilesets look a bit dated and bland, and even though data-wise they don't seem to lag behind GMaps too much, presentation matters and the user experience is just not as polished. They both are perfectly usable though. Quantmaps might one day have a user experience closer to the one Google delivers now, but as for now, but as for now, it's just not ready. For now, I think I'll replace Google Maps with Here Maps and their mobile app, but I'm is that not 100% satisfied. I'll be keeping my eye on QuantMaps, which seems to have the right approach of simplicity and good design. When it's full-featured, it will probably be my mapping service of choice. Do you know of any other map providers that could replace Google Maps? Let me know in the comments! In the meantime, I hope you guys enjoyed it and I'll see you guys in the next one. Bye! If you enjoyed, please consider liking, subscribing, and turning on notifications. You can also follow me on Twitter at theLinuxEXP Thank you guys for watching and goodbye!

I'm still looking for alternatives to popular Google services, just to see if it would be feasible to not have all my data in one provider's hand. In this one, I'm going to take a look at map services. Google Maps Google maps is widely known. It's probably the richest map data-wise, with the added benefit of street view, a well-stocked satellite view, data from points of interest and businesses, and a good interface. We're going to take a look at other services, with the requirements that they use something other than Google maps for data. I'm not expecting a Street view replacement in any of these alternatives. Open Street Maps OSM is like the wikipedia of maps, with anyone being able to contribute to it, trace roads, buildings, and add points of interests, and more. OSM is accessible from their website, www.openstreetmap.org, and has the basics, such as directions, and search. It lacks a satellite view, street view, and doesn't have any informations about businesses. It also doesn't have the most elegant tile set there is. MapQuest uses the OSM database to build their maps. It's been around for a while, but it seems more focused on the US market. Qwant Maps use OSM as well, but it's still an alpha-level product. It doesn't have a mobile application, and doesn't have directions yet. It does look nice, and has basic informations when clicking on any POI, with favorites support. On smartphones, the choice is a bit more varied, and that's what matters. OSMAnd seems to be the best choice out there on Android, with downloadable maps for offline access, and a ton of different

options including which points of interest you want to display, the look of the map, a dark theme, a car GPS mode, and many more. It's also interesting to note that there is a project called Open Street Cam which aims to provide an alternative to Street View. Here Maps Here Maps was formerly a Nokia product. They provide a web interface, as well as a mobile app, called Here We Go. The web interface is pretty slow to load tiles, and returned a very limited set of Point of interests, in my tests. It does have a few informations on each of them, though, so that's a plus. It has directions, which are actually pretty well done, letting you choose between car, bike, on foot, as well as ride sharing or even a taxi. It also has a satellite view, and can even show some public transportation information. Here maps also have access to traffic information in certain cities. The mobile app is alright, it is pretty clear right at startup about what kind of data it collects, and has most of what you'd expect, including directions, favorites, and traffic data. It also can change the view mode from normal to satellite, and even download offline maps, if you're preparing a trip abroad and want to make sure you'll get a functioning GPS service. Here maps is a good proposition that could definitely replace Google Maps in my admitedly simple uses. Bing Maps Bing Maps is Microsoft's map service. It's a smaller proposition, including only a web interface and no mobile application. Bing maps has points of interest with a lot of data supplied by TripAdvisor, and local data providers, such as

Pages Jaunes in France. It has pretty complete directions, including the ability to avoid highways or ferries, and it has traffic data to help you navigate or use it as a GPS while driving. Bing Maps also supports a satellite view, and what they call "streetside", which is a street view equivalent. It seems to work in major cities, for example, in France, Paris had a pretty good coverage, but this feature is not available as widely as Google's. Bing Maps doesn't seem to have a mobile application though, which is a shame, since it's where most people will use it anyway. All in all, Bing maps is probably the best proposition on the web, outside of Google Maps, but without a mobile application to use, I just could not see myself switching to it. Other alternatives The first is Wikimapia, a collaborative effort to give free maps to anyone who might need them. It's distributed under the open source Creative Communs BY-SA license. Yandex Maps is also a good proposition, but if you're trying to escape the internet giants, the Russian Google might not be the best choice. Duck Duck Go uses Apple Maps, which looks good, but they don't provide a separate map service. All in all, while Here Maps and Bing Maps are pretty good, I still feel they lack the polish and overall nice finish of Google Maps. Their tilesets look a bit dated and bland, and even though data-wise, they don't seem to lag behind Gmaps too much, presentation matters, and the user experience is not as polished. They both are perfectly usable though. Qwant Maps might one day have a user experience closer to the one
Google delivers, but as of now, it's just not ready. For now, I'll replace Google Maps with Here Maps, but I'm not 100% satisfied. Follow me on Twitter : http://twitter.com/thelinuxEXP

OpenStreetMaps. OSM is like the Wikipedia of maps, with anyone being able to contribute to it, trace roads, buildings and app points of interests and more. OSM is accessible from their website openStreetMap.org and has the basics such as directions and search. It lacks a satellite view, streetview and doesn't have any information about businesses, which is uses besides simple routing. It also doesn't have the most elegant tile-set there is. The colors are muted, it lacks legibility and is generally not very appealing. Fortunately, since OSM is open-source, a few providers have built their own tile-sets and

features off of it. You most notably can use GNOME Maps or Marble to access it from the desktop app on Linux. So what map provider use OpenStreetMaps? Well, we get MapQuest, which uses the OpenStreetMap database to build their maps. It's been around for a while, but it seems more focused on the US market, and doesn't return any useful data for France, for example. Quantmaps uses OSM as well, and it's still an alpha-level product. It doesn't have a mobile application product, doesn't have an app and not yet got directions. It does look nice, and has basic information when clicking on any path with favourite support but is just too limited. This might, at some point, be a very valid alternative, but for now, it just lacks too many features. As of now there doesn't seem to be a full-on web implementation of OpenStreetMaps with Points of Interests, Directions, and Satellite View. OpenStreetMap is mostly used by service providers to sell this kind of package for integration in other services, but they don't seem to provide a free online mapping service. On smartphones, the choice is a bit more varied, and that's what matters, because this is where you're going to be using these maps most of the time. OSM ONT seems to be the best choice out there on Android with downloadable maps for offline access, and a ton of different options, including which point of interest you wanna display, the look of the map, a dark theme, a car GPS mode, and many more… It's also interesting to note that there is a project called OpenStreetCam, which aims to provide an alternative to Streetview, but

its interface is a bit cumbersome and, since it's sourced by users, it's not as complete and well detailed. Still it's a great project that should definitely be integrated directly into the OSM interface to give it more visibility. HairMaps HairMaps was formerly a Nokia product and is now operated by a consortium of auto manufacturers they provide a web interface as well as a mobile app called here we go the web interface is pretty slow to load tiles and return a very limited set of point of interests in my tests it does have a few informations on each of them though so there's a plus. It has directions, which are actually pretty well done, letting you choose between car, bike, on foot, as well as ride-sharing or even a taxi. It also has a satellite view and can even show some public transportation information, such as the path they will take. In my hometown, Brest, I could see the itinerary their streetcars take, but not the bus lines. And in Paris they have all metro lines for example. Heron Maps also have access to traffic information in certain cities but it does not have a Street View implementation. The mobile application called here we go is alright, it is pretty clear right at start up about what kind of data it collects and it has most of what you'd expect, including directions, favorites and traffic data. It also can change the view mode from Normal to Satellite and even download off-line maps if you're preparing a trip abroad and want to make sure you'll get a functioning GPS service. Here Maps doesn't look very good in my opinion, but it gets the job done. In

general it's not a bad service, but the slow loading of tiles and the inertia while dragging the map was a bit annoying. HairMaps is a good proposition that could definitely replace Google Maps in my admittedly simple uses. Bing Maps Bing Maps is Microsoft's Map service. It is a smaller proposition, including only a web interface and no mobile application. Bing Maps has points of interest with a lot of data supplied by Tripadvisor, and local data providers such as Pagone in France. It has pretty complete directions, including the ability to avoid highways or ferries and it has traffic data to help you navigate or use it as a GPS while driving Bing maps supports satellite view, and what they call Streetsight which is a Street View equivalent It seems to work in major cities, for example in France, Paris has a good coverage. But this feature isn't as widely available as Google's Bing Maps doesn't seem to have a mobile application though, which is a shame. Since it's one where most people will use it anyway More aggravating? There is no mobile version of Bing Maps at all, not even a mobile website or at least I couldn't find it. This is a big oversight that makes the service instantly less accessible and useful. All in all, Bing maps is probably the best proposition on the web outside of Google Maps but without a mobile application to use I just could not see myself switching to it. Other alternatives. Apart from these big ones, there are a few other alternatives that deserve a mention. The first is Wikimapia, a collaborative effort to give free maps to anyone who might need

them. It's distributed under the open-source Creative Commons BYSA license. While its interface is not up to par and the data volume seems pretty low where I live it's definitely something to keep an eye on. Yandex maps is also a good proposition but if you're trying to escape the internet giants the Russian Google might not be the best choice for you. DuckduckGo uses apple maps which looks good, but they don't provide a separate map service. It's just used to illustrate and locate their search results. You can't actually use the map as you would google maps. You are limited to browsing it, switching the view but it doesn't have any directions or point of interest details. All in all, while hero maps and big maps are pretty good I still feel they like the polish and overall nice finish of Google Maps. Their tilesets look a bit dated and bland, and even though data-wise they don't seem to lag behind GMaps too much, presentation matters and the user experience is just not as polished. They both are perfectly usable though. Quantmaps might one day have a user experience closer to the one Google delivers now, but as for now, but as for now, it's just not ready. For now, I think I'll replace Google Maps with Here Maps and their mobile app, but I'm is that not 100% satisfied. I'll be keeping my eye on QuantMaps, which seems to have the right approach of simplicity and good design. When it's full-featured, it will probably be my mapping service of choice.
